content: Planetary science, also referred to as planetology and closely associated with planetary astronomy, is the scientific study of planets, planetary systems, and the Solar System. This field employs an interdisciplinary approach, integrating knowledge from various scientific disciplines. It can be considered a subset of Earth sciences or, more appropriately, its parent field. Research in planetary science typically involves a combination of astronomy, space exploration (especially robotic spacecraft missions), and comparative, experimental, and meteoritic studies conducted on Earth. Theoretical modeling and computer simulations also play a significant role in advancing the field. A major component of planetary science is astrogeology, which focuses on the geological aspects of celestial bodies. Planetology has evolved as an interdisciplinary science, emerging from astronomy and Earth sciences, and its development has been driven by advancements in robotics and measurement technologies. Planetary science encompasses the study of planets, their moons, and all other bodies and radiations within the Solar System. It also examines the various force fields and interactions among the components of the Solar System. A new discipline within Earth sciences, known as geonomy, is closely related to planetary science. Geonomy synthesizes and integrates knowledge from various Earth science disciplines. However, the sequence of data collection differs between Earth sciences and planetary science. Earth sciences began with studies in the immediate vicinity of humans and gradually expanded to encompass the entire planet. In contrast, planetary science originated in astronomy, initially focusing on the study of planets as points of light and later achieving higher resolution observations of atmospheric and surface details. The Moon, due to its proximity, has always been an exception, as its surface details have been observable even with early telescopes. Over time, improved resolution has led to increasingly detailed geological knowledge of the Moon, facilitated by astronomical telescopes, radio telescopes, and robotic space probes. Planetary science integrates various disciplines, including those traditionally focused on terrestrial studies, such as mineralogy, petrology, and geochemistry. This has given rise to subfields like cosmochemistry, cosmopetrology, and cosmo-geochemistry. Meteoritics, a branch of planetary science, studies the rocky and mineral materials of the Solar System. Key journals in this field include Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta and Meteoritics and Planetary Science. The most significant annual conference in planetary science is the Lunar and Planetary Science Conference (LPSC), organized by the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Houston at NASA's Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center. Since its inception in 1970, the LPSC has been a cornerstone of the field. One of the most prominent research areas in planetary science involves the study of the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and Venus, which are the planetary bodies closest to Earth. The Moon was the first celestial body where methods developed for Earth studies were applied. Two key disciplines in surface studies are geomorphology and stratigraphy. Geomorphology focuses on the features of planetary surfaces and reconstructs the processes that formed them. It includes studies of features resulting from external impacts, such as multi-ringed basins and craters, as well as those originating from internal processes like volcanism and tectonism, such as lava flows, fissures, and rilles. Additionally, it examines erosional features produced by continuous meteorite bombardment. On the Moon, impact structures range from large basins with diameters of 1,000 kilometers to micrometer-sized craterlets on mineral grains. Volcanism on the Moon has created extensive lava flows with wrinkle ridges and lava channels, providing morphological evidence of their formation. Erosion on the Moon has resulted in a thin regolith dust cover on its surface. Geomorphological studies help decipher the history of planetary surfaces by mapping features according to their stratigraphic sequence, a method first established on Earth by Nicolas Steno. Stratigraphic mapping was instrumental in preparing Apollo astronauts for their lunar missions. Stratigraphy involves studying and arranging strata based on their settling sequence and summarizing them in stratigraphic maps. Geological axioms were developed to identify strata and determine their sequence, and these principles were applied to the Moon. Overlapping sequences were initially identified through images and photometric and telescopic measurements, later enhanced by remote sensing technologies like the Lunar Orbiter. The culmination of this work was the creation of a lunar stratigraphic column, which outlines the sequence of major strata and the events that produced them, along with a stratigraphic map of the Moon. The youngest stratigraphic unit on the Moon is the Copernican unit, characterized by rayed impact craters. Below this are craters without ray systems but with well-developed impact crater morphology, belonging to the Eratosthenian unit. The two youngest units are found in crater-sized spots on the Moon. Beneath them are the mare units (previously defined as the Procellarian unit) and the Imbrium basin-related ejecta and tectonic units (Imbrian units). Another impact basin-related unit is the Nectarian unit, centered around the Nectarian Basin. At the base of the lunar stratigraphic sequence lies the pre-Nectarian unit, consisting of old crater plains. Mercury's surface and stratigraphy share many similarities with the Moon. A branch of planetary science focuses on the study of rocky and mineral materials from planetary bodies with rigid surfaces. These materials come from three main sources: meteorites, lunar samples, and Martian samples. Meteorites were the first known extraterrestrial materials. For over 200 years, they have been collected and studied to gather data about their parent bodies. Most meteorites originate from smaller asteroidal bodies in the Solar System, making them valuable for studying the evolution of these bodies. Chondrites, in particular, are significant as they contain chondrules (small spherical grains) and represent primordial materials from the early Solar System. During the Apollo program, lunar samples were collected and transported to Earth, totaling 384 kilograms. Additionally, three Luna robots delivered regolith samples from the Moon. Lunar meteorites have also been discovered among Antarctic meteorites, with approximately 100 paired lunar meteorites known as of 2008. Martian meteorites represent the third group of planetary materials. As of 2008, around 50 paired Martian meteorites have been identified. Space probes have enabled the collection of data across the electromagnetic spectrum, allowing the study of the outer, sparsely populated material space around planets. Planets are characterized by their force fields, including gravity and magnetic fields. Magnetic fields interact with the solar wind to form magnetospheres around planets with strong magnetic fields. Early space probes revealed the main aspects of Earth's magnetic field, which extends about 10 Earth radii toward the Sun. The Sun's corpuscular radiations stream around Earth's magnetic field, forming a magnetic chamber (magnetosphere) and a magnetic tail extending hundreds of Earth radii. Inside the magnetosphere, radiation belts (Van Allen belts) form, where charged particle density is high. The gravity fields of planets have been studied using the spatial acceleration of space probes, revealing fine details. For example, gravity field disturbances above lunar maria led to the discovery of mascons (mass concentrations) in the 1970s. Five lunar mascons were identified in the Imbrium, Serenitatis, Crisium, Nectaris, and Humorum basins. The rotational force field of planets also affects their atmospheres. Not all planets have atmospheres, as their existence depends on the planet's mass. Besides the four giant planets, Earth, Venus, Mars, and Saturn's moon Titan have atmospheres. Planetary rotation influences body shape and atmospheric streams, as seen in the striped cloud systems of Jupiter and Saturn, observable even with amateur telescopes. These atmospheric belts are analogous to terrestrial Hadley cells. Comparative planetary science examines the evolutionary paths of Solar System bodies, which formed under different initial conditions, such as composition, mass, and solar distance. This discipline compares the evolutionary histories of individual objects, using planetary bodies as natural laboratories. Decades of future space probe investigations are needed to construct detailed evolutionary histories of planetary bodies. Comparative studies can help fill gaps in known histories. For instance, lunar history has provided insights into the first three aeons of Solar System events, which were largely erased on Earth. Planetary science investigates objects ranging in size from micrometeoroids to gas giants, focusing on their composition, dynamics, and history.
